gaps.sentence: This time next week I ___ on a beach in Portugal, with my phone switched off.
gaps.hint: this time next week means in progress
gaps.explanation: 'This time next week' points to an action in progress at a future moment, so the future continuous fits: will be lying.

gaps.sentence: He ___ very shy at first, but once you know him he is very chatty.
gaps.hint: seem describes a state not action
gaps.explanation: 'Seem' describes a state and is not used continuously: seems.

gaps.sentence: My grandfather ___ walk five miles to school when he was a boy.
gaps.hint: a past habit no longer true
gaps.explanation: 'Used to' describes past habits or states that are no longer true: used to walk.

gaps.sentence: The audience always ___ when the curtain falls.
gaps.explanation: 'Always' marks a general habit, which takes the present simple: claps.

gaps.sentence: I ___ the dentist on Thursday afternoon — I booked it last week.
gaps.explanation: A personal arrangement already made takes the present continuous: am seeing.

gaps.sentence: We ___ each other since primary school, so nothing surprises me about him.
gaps.hint: since primary school continuing to now
gaps.explanation: A state continuing since a past point takes the present perfect: have known.

gaps.sentence: Look at the time! We ___ for over two hours.
gaps.hint: for over two hours up to now
gaps.explanation: A duration continuing up to the present moment takes the present perfect continuous: have been chatting.

gaps.sentence: This is the best pizza I ___ in years.
gaps.hint: superlative experience counted up to now
gaps.explanation: Superlative statements about experience up to now take the present perfect: have eaten.
